name: Memory & bandwidth (HBM)
summary: How fast data reaches the chip often limits AI speed more than the chip's raw arithmetic.

D1.guide: Watch the narrow door. Does a faster cook help if ingredients arrive slowly?
text: Imagine a super-fast cook who has to wait for ingredients to come through a narrow door. The cook's speed doesn't matter if the door is slow.
For AI, the ingredients are the model's numbers, and the door is memory bandwidth.
D1.analogy: A fast cook waiting at a narrow pantry door.

text: Generating each token means reading the model's active weights from memory. If those weights take tens of gigabytes, every new token moves that much data. On a home machine, whether those weights fit in fast memory at all is the first question (see [local AI hardware](#/concept/local-ai-hardware)).
High-bandwidth memory (HBM) stacks memory chips right next to the processor so data moves far faster than with ordinary memory.
Rule of thumb for a single user: tokens per second is roughly memory bandwidth divided by the bytes of weights read per token.
D2.analogy: A narrow door between the pantry and the kitchen.
D2.analogyBreaks: A pantry door moves each ingredient once. A model's weights are re-read for every single token, so the same data crosses the 'door' over and over; batching many users shares each trip.

predict.question: You halve the size of a model's weights (16-bit to 8-bit) on the same hardware. Roughly what happens to single-user generation speed?
predict.explanation: If generation is limited by memory reads, moving half as many bytes per token roughly doubles tokens per second; in practice a bit less.

text: Where it's heading: faster HBM generations, designs with much more on-chip memory, and algorithmic tricks such as speculative decoding that get more tokens out of each memory read.

sources.title: Roofline: an insightful visual performance model (Williams, Waterman, Patterson)
